title: 14 B.C. premiers have now signed this one-of-a-kind $1 bill since 1971
summary: Every time Earl Brown has met a B.C. premier, he's had them sign the same one-dollar bill. It was first signed by W.A.C. Bennett in 1971, and this week, he added Lorne Doerkson's signature to his…

image.caption: Fort Nelson resident Earl Brown shows off his dollar bill filled with the signatures of 14 B.C. premiers. (Matt Preprost/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Every time Earl Brown has met a B.C. premier, he's had them sign the same one-dollar bill. It was first signed by W.A.C. Bennett in 1971, and this week, he added Lorne Doerkson's signature to his collection.
Fort Nelson resident says new premiers have been eager to add their names to his priceless banknote
Earl Brown has spent the past 55 years passing the buck to B.C. politicians.
Literally.
And this past week, he wasted no time doing so to newly-minted Premier Lorne Doerkson.
Three days after Doerkson was sworn in at Government House in Victoria, Brown, a longtime Fort Nelson resident, dropped into his constituency office in Williams Lake with an unusual request.
"I've got this dollar bill I need to be signed by the premier. Do you have any premiers in stock?" Brown recalled asking Doerkson's assistant.
Brown was passing through town from Salmon Arm and looking to add a 14th signature to a $1 bill that he's been using to collect signatures from B.C. premiers since he was a kid.

items: Premier Lorne Doerkson sworn in alongside 1st B.C. Conservative cabinet

blocks.text: Much to Brown's surprise, Doerkson just so happened to be in the office.
Though he was running late for a flight, Doerkson couldn't pass on taking part in what's become a storied B.C. tradition.
"At the time, I felt nothing short of euphoric," said Brown. "It was an absolute delight to have managed to go ahead and secure that."
Every time Earl Brown has met a B.C. premier, he's had them sign the same $1 bill. It was first signed by premier W.A.C. Bennett, who he met in 1971 when he was 14 years old. (Matt Preprost/CBC)
Brown was 14 when he snagged his first political autograph.
It was September 1971 when then-premier W.A.C. Bennett was in Fort Nelson for the opening of the PGE Railway.
There was just one problem.
Brown brought nothing for Bennett to write on.
"He said, 'Sure. Where's your autograph book?'" Brown recalled. "I said, 'Uh oh, wait a second, here, maybe you could sign this $1 bill for me?
"And he took a $1 bill out of his own billfold, signed that, handed it to me ... Some people said I'm one of the few people that got Bennett for a buck."

Earl Brown with his mom, Mavis, when he was just 14 and welcoming the arrival of the inaugural Pacific Great Eastern Railway train in Fort Nelson, B.C. in 1971. It was here where he snagged his first political autograph, from then premier W.A.C. Bennett. (Earl Brown)
By the end of the 1970s, Brown had added the signatures of Dave Barrett and Bennett's son, Bill, to the back of the banknote.
That's when Brown said he knew it was a tradition meant to continue, each signature telling its own unique story.

Rita Johnston scribbled a doodle in a corner to get her pen working.
Ujjal Dosanjh signed "the day before he was decimated at the polls."
John Horgan, meanwhile, was so enthralled that Brown's 10-minute appointment quickly turned into half an hour, as Horgan proudly showed off the bill to others in his office in Victoria.

B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson with Fort Nelson resident Earl Brown after adding his signature to Brown's one-of-a-kind one-dollar bill that has become a gallery of autographs from the province's premiers. (Sue Brown)
The banknote even has its own political geography.
New Democrats, naturally, have all signed on the left. Christy Clark, reluctant to sign below Bill Vander Zalm, chose the right edge, Brown said.
He pointed this out to Doerkson.
"I said most of the NDP premiers have all signed on the left, and he said, 'Well, I'm certainly not going to be doing that.'"
So Doerkson signed the bottom right corner instead and added something none of his predecessors had. The number 38, denoting himself as B.C.'s 38th premier.
"I found all of the premiers to be fairly approachable, even when I sometimes caught them with almost no notice," said Brown.
"Now that the thing has got its own little story and so forth, there's quite an eagerness."
The late B.C. premier John Horgan admires the history on Earl Brown's 'Premier's Buck.' (Earl Brown)
Brown said he and his wife Sue are working on a children's book about what he calls his "Premier's Buck."
He hopes to have it finished by next summer.

As for the bill itself, Brown figures it will eventually find a home in a museum.
If and when it does, will it include a 15th signature?
"I'm not sure if there's any more room," Brown said.
"You go ahead and put 14 signatures on a piece of paper that's six by almost three inches, you fill that sucker up pretty [quickly], so we'll see what happens."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
